subtopic: PROPOSED DEDUCTION OP TEN PEIS CENT IN INDEMNITIES AND SALARIES

speechtext:
Hon. E. N. RHODES (Minister of Finance) moved the second reading of Bill No. 19, to provide for the reduction of compensation in the public service.
He said: Mr. Speaker, the principle underlying this bill was discussed so fully when the resolution upon which it is founded was under consideration that I do not think at this stage I can add anything to what I said on that occasion. I am content therefore merely to move the second reading and to reserve to myself an opportunity to discuss in detail in committee any questions which may arise.

subtopic: PROPOSED DEDUCTION OP TEN PEIS CENT IN INDEMNITIES AND SALARIES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the bill now before the house is to provide for the reduction of compensation in the public service. On the introduction of the resolution I gave a number of reasons why, in my mind, the measure should not pass. When the resolution was introduced I expressed the hope that the bill to follow, which would be founded upon the resolution, might contain some alterations. I am sorry to say, however, that that is not so, that the bill is framed in the same terms as the resolution. I am sorely disappointed, and must quote the words of Virgil, una salus victis nullam sperare salutem-that to the vanquished there is but one hope of salvation, to hope for no salvation.
On second thought I am not very much surprised that the bill is as radical as was the resolution. After witnessing what has happened in this house during the past two weeks, after seeing a demonstration of the theory that might is right, I can expect nothing more than a bill in the terms of the one now before us. I say this bill is economically unsound because it purports to produce revenue through a reduction in purchasing power. It is economically unsound because it purports to create economy in one sphere, namely, in the national budget, by reducing the purchasing power of 65,000 civil servants throughout the country, and by reducing that same power in a large number of other portions of the population. It is economically unsound because it strikes at the very root of contractual obligations between master and servant. On a former occasion, however, I went extensively into that phase of the matter. It 
is economically unsound because it is of an extraordinary nature and should not have been resorted to until all other means had failed. It is equivalent to a measure of taxation, and hits hardest those least able to bear the burden; in other words, all will have to pay at the same rate. The father supporting a wife and family will pay the same as a married man with no family. The widow with dependent children will pay the same as the civil servant who, with no dependents, lives in security and comfort. The son or daughter supporting a widowed mother or invalid father will pay the same as other sons or daughters living at ease. At page 59 of Hansard the Prime Minister is reported as follows:
-and desiring that the people of this country should understand fully that the government is anxious to lead the way with respect to matters of economy.
Sir, he has said the government is anxious to lead the way in matters of economy. There is no great skill in the announcement of the policy we are now discussing. Anyone can effect economy in his business by cutting the wages of his employees. The real test of the skilled administrator is to devise and put into effect such policies as will be beneficial to business interests, will produce increased profit, will put more money into circulation, increase employment and thereby increase revenues and extend trade. The Prime Minister went about his task in the wrong way. His policies have killed our trade. Decreased trade and decreased revenues have increased unemployment. Now the right hon. gentleman proceeds to cure unemployment by creating more unemployment.
The statement has been made that the very best antidote for poison is an extra dose of the same poison. I am told, however, that great skill is required in the administration of such remedies, and I submit the right hon gentleman has showed himself to be a very poor medical practitioner in the administration of medicines or remedies to cure our national ills. Then, we understand the reduction in salaries is made for the purpose of enabling the Prime Minister to balance his budget. He may balance it in the way of dollars and cents, but he is not taking into account the physical difficulties he is creating. He is not taking into account the mental and moral anguish which will follow in the wake of this legislation. He may balance his budget in dollars and cents, but he cannot balance the national budget when the individuals composing the nation are without work and are starving. People must be contented both morally and financially. There can be no balancing of a budget unless the

Public Service-Salary Deduction
individuals in the country enjoy a perfect state of happiness and contentment. There can be no balancing of a budget at a cost of starvation and privation due to reduced wages and lack of work.
The government has been sorely remiss in its duty when it has attempted to effect a balance at these costs. If a way cannot be blasted into the markets of the world the Prime Minister will blast his way into the pockets of the civil servants. Unable to blast his way into the markets of the world the Prime Minister will now blast open the doors of, and blast his way into the homes of the civil servants. No easier method could have been found than simply to tell his Minister of Finance to do a little juggling with the decimal point. In connection with the $93,000,000 paid to the civil servants he would simply move the decimal point a few places to the right and receive the benefit of the accrued revenue. Civil servants throughout Canada are being asked to contribute their share of the payment of the national debt. Are the people at the head of our large institutions doing the same thing? If the E. B. Eddy Company cut the salaries and wages of their employees, will they take that money and bring it to the Minister of Finance to lay beside the moneys collected through deductions from civil servants' salaries to be applied towards the satisfaction of the national debt?
Not only that, but we know the example set by the government will be followed throughout the country. Following the lead given by the Prime Minister, other employers of labour will make cuts. The money saved through wages cut in the ordinary course of business will not be added as special revenues to help pay the national debt. The few millions which would be collected in that way would be but a drop in the bucket as compared with the hundreds of millions of dollars of national debt. I cannot appreciate the idea behind the horizontal cut, that if, due to the depression, some people must suffer, those who are more fortunate should also suffer. In other words, I cannot understand why, if I should be suffering, I should insist that my neighbour suffer also, even though that suffering might alleviate my own. Certainly there is no warrant for my asking someone else to suffer while that suffering will not help me at all. I fail to realize the force of the argument that because the farmers are having a hard time, or because the financial situation is a difficult one, the civil service throughout Canada should also feel the pinch. I should think the spirit of solidarity should prevail and that we should rejoice in the fact
that during this period of depression the hard times are not felt by the entire population of Canada.
I say that these reductions in salary and these cuts in the personnel of the civil service strike at the very foundation of civil service institutions. Some day, when it is too late, the effects of this policy will be seen. I have not time to deal with each of the topics on which I had intended to speak, but I do want to point out that it is most imperative that the civil service of Canada should be maintained at its present high standing. I have no less authority for that statement than the report of the Beatty commission, which at page 9 contains the following words:
The formal distinction between the legislative and executive branches of government, between parliament on the one hand and the cabinet controlling administration on the other, obscures but it does not alter the fact that efficient parliamentary government is only possible when the decisions embodied in statutory form are made effective throughout the dominion by a body of trained administrators and experts.
Further down the page I find the following:
The problems of government are becoming ever more complex; the effectiveness of government action must Ire limited, to a substantial extent, by the quality of the civil service, which is called upon to investigate many subjects of national importance demanding consideration by the government, as well as to make governmental policies effective and governmental decisions operative; and we believe that no more important task confronts those in charge of the country's affairs, than that of improving, and continuing to improve, by every means at their disposal, the quality of the civil service of Canada.
-not to wreck it at every opportunity. Then on page 10 the report states:
Throughout our inquiries we have been impressed by the character of the work now done in the civil service of Canada. In accord with the highest traditions to be found elsewhere, its own tradition demands the faithful performance of his duties by the individual, though the results of the' work done, however important they may be, do not accrue directly to him, either in the form of wealth, or, as a rule, in the form of public recognition.
The quotation is most interesting, but it is rather lengthy. Then on page 11 I find the following:
It is essential to the continued welfare of the country that the civil service be enabled continuously to recruit workers with a proper scientific equipment for their tasks, and to retain them in the face of the high rewards offered for work of the same character elsewhere.


Public Service-Salary Deduction
Here is a most interesting extract from page 13:
.... in the past the civil service has been successful in enlisting and retaining men of first rate ability, despite the relatively moderate remuneration. We do not feel the same assurance, however, that it will continue successfully to recruit or hold such men in the future, unless conditions of employment and prospects of advancement in the service can be simplified and improved considerably.
Then they talk about those three factors so dear to the heart of the Prime Minister, security of tenure, superannuation and holidays and sick leave. I quote from page 14:
These three conditions serve, very properly, to assist in relieving the civil servant of anxieties with regard to his own future and that of his dependents; and so set him free, without such distractions, to concentrate upon his duties. But while they do constitute advantages, when compared with the conditions ordinarily prevailing in private employment, such advantages are not those which as a rule appeal most strongly to men of an energetic, creative temperament, among whom the leaders in the service, no less than the directing heads of private enterprises, must be sought. For the sake of the country, no less than of the service itself, it is necessary that conditions of employment should offer a permanent positive attraction to men of this type.
The very fabric, sir, of the civil service throughout Canada is being jeopardized forever by these continual dismissals, made in hit and miss fashion, and by these unwarranted, unjust, unfair and inequitable deductions. I say, sir, that the service is not in a position to bear this reduction. No one earning a moderate salary, such as the majority of civil servants earn, is in a position to stand this cut. A return was brought down recently which shows that 42.5 per cent of the permanent civil service of Canada earn up to SI,500 yearly, while 79.5 per cent of civil servants earn less than $2,000 a year. Those figures should be kept in mind.
When I spoke previously on this question the Minister of Finance said in reply that the only equitable way was to have a horizontal cut. Let me give a concrete illustration. In this house we as members are cut ten per cent; my S400 will lie next to the Prime Minister's $1,900, but that is done by virtue of an arbitrary rule. If a graded cut were made whereby the Prime Minister and myself paid according to our respective means, my $400 would not be $400, and the Prime Minister's $1,900 would not be $1,900! It is true that on the other hand the Prime Minister will pay a tax on his income, but I will have to pay an income tax of my own, so in that respect we are equal, because the income tax is based 
upon the capacity to pay. This ten per cent reduction, however, is an arbitrary rule disregarding the capacity to earn or to pay.
To follow that example through let us consider the civil servant who earns $3,600 a year. He is not yet at his maximum; this year he is entitled to a statutory increase of $120, but what will happen? First he will suffer a loss of $360, or ten per cent of his salary; in addition he will be deprived of his annual increase of $120, amounting to another three per cent, and in addition five per cent of his salary is deducted for superannuation, which would amount to $190. Therefore this civil servant will be mulcted to the extent of $670. It is true that his contribution to the superannuation fund ultimately will come back to him, but for the time being he suffers a deduction of 18 per cent, and in addition he will have to pay income tax on whatever is left of the $3,600 after the deductions are allowed. Right away that civil servant suffers a deduction of 18 per cent, while hon. members of this house suffer a loss of ten per cent.
I am further opposed to the passage of this legislation, because, as I say, it prejudicially affects the interests of this constituency, and I have no apology to offer for taking up the cudgels on behalf of the very large proportion of civil servants who live in the city of Ottawa, any more than I have anything to say against anyone who takes the part of any particular class in his community whose privileges and rights do not in any way conflict with the general wellbeing of that community. In this city the ordinary citizens have certain rights and privileges, and the civil servants, as a particular class, have particular rights and privileges, and as such they have the right to be taken into account. Therefore, I make no apology for taking up the cudgels, as I do, on behalf of that class, just as I would do on behalf of any other special class constituting a minority but with special rights, provided that those rights did not clash in any way with the rights and general interests of the community at large. Ottawa has a population of 130,000 inhabitants. On the 31st of March 1931 there were 11,766 employees of the civil service residing in Ottawa, of whom 8,009 were permanents and 3,757 were temporaries. The civil servants' ipay-roll for that year in Ottawa was $19,134,162; it is now, in round figures, $20,000,000, because of statutory increases granted last year but not granted this year. Now, ten per cent of $20,000,000 is $2,000,000, and the statutory increases cut off this year ajmount to about $500,000. Therefore Ottawa

Public Service-Salary Deduction
will be deprived this year of the sum of $2,500,000. Bad as that is. it might be tolerated with great difficulty, with great misery a.nd anguish. But we know that in trade a dollar is worth three dollars in turnover; so that during the coming year Ottawa will suffer a loss, not of $2,500,000 but of $7,500,0000. Now what does that mean? It means absolute catastrophe financially for the city of Ottawa It means that $2,500,000 is to be taken from the earning capacity of 12.000 people in a population of 130,000. Can hon. gentlemen realize what that means? Do they realize what it means to have $2,500,000 levied upon
12.000	people living in a community of 130,000? It means that every man, woman and child, every head in the city of Ottawa will suffer a tax of $19, and every civil servant in the city will be taxed to the extent of $209.
The Prime Minister stated, as reported at page 562 of Hansard:
There will accrue to the revenues approximately $8,300,000.
He will therefore obtain $2,500,000 from Ottawa, leaving $6,000,000 to be derived from sources outsides this city. That $6,000,000 will be levied on 62,000 employees, less the
12.000	in Ottawa, or on 50,000 employees distributed among a population of 10,000,000. This means that every one of the civil servants outside Ottawa will contribute on an average $120; but the population outside Ottawa will feel it to the extent of 60 cents per head, as compared with $19 in this city.
Of course, it will be pointed out that if all the civil servants resided in Ottawa, Ottawa alone would have to bear the burden. That is perfectly true; but is that any reason why this city should be made to suffer in the way I have indicated? If the Prime Minister and his government had had in mind an equitable measure they would have seen to it that this cut would be, not horizontal but graded, in order to alleviate the blow that has been struck at this community. Up to March 2 there were in Ottawa, according to the records of the city hall, 6,286 registered unemployed. But that does not take into consideration all those that do not register. It does not take into consideration the 169 who have been let out of the air force; it does not take into consideration the 82 artisans who have been let out of the Public Works the first of this month it does not take into consideration the 313 Department of the Interior employees who have not been reabsorbed into the service; it does not take into consideration the 150 other employees let out in this happy-go-lucky, hit or miss fashion;
41761-106J
and it does not take into consideration those who will be let out within the next few months.
This, sir, is a situation that is very far from being reassuring. The Prime Minister stated, as reported at page 561 of Hansard:
The Canadian Pacific Railway Company a year ago instituted such economies; the Canadian National Railways last year instituted economies in that direction; and further economies have been effected by the findings of boards in connection with the running trades. Recently a board was sitting in Montreal when its duties were suddenly ended by an agreement being arrived at whereby a ten per cent reduction was accepted by the clerical staffs of the railways, the question then being under consideration by a conciliation board.
That is true, and with that I have not much quarrel. But why did not the Prime Minister listen to the representations that were being made by the civil service organizations, or which they were trying to make? Why did he not listen when they came to him that morning? I am not so sure he did not tell them that they ought to consider themselves lucky that they did not suffer a more severe cut. I am not so sure he did not tell them that they ought to "give until it hurts." The Prime Minister was right in using the language I have just quoted with reference to the Canadian Pacific Railway. But let me point out that the quotation includes the findings of boards. A board was sitting, an agreement was arrived at, and the reduction was accepted. There was a conciliation board, but the Prime Minister never granted a board of conciliation-

That is correct as

But if they had no agreement with the clerical staffs, then my remarks apply to them also; and I say that the right hon. gentleman should have listened to the representations made on behalf of the civil servants, just as the Canadian National Railways and the Canadian Pacific Railway should have taken their employees into consideration in an endeavour to arrive at some human understanding whereby the reduction might have been graded. Because the Canadian Pacific Railway or the Canadian National Railways did not do it right in one connection, although they did in another, is no excuse for the right hon. gentleman to think that he is at liberty to take the wrong course in every direction.
The right hon. gentleman is reported on page 561 of Hansard as having said that the cost of living to-day is about 14-4 per cent lower than it was in 1926. I am not concerned with what the cost of living was in 1926, I am concerned only with the cost to-day. I had intended to go into the different phases of the economic feature of this question, but this has been done quite fully by the hon. member for Bow River (Mr. Garland). The Labour Gazette of February, 1932, shows the cost of living for December, 1931, as S17.76, and for the end of January, 1932, as $17.59, a difference of less than one per cent. Rent has not come down, fuel and light have not come down, the cost of food has come down very little, insurance rates on life and fire have not come down nor have telephone rates. The right hon. gentleman has had telephones taken out of the Supreme Court building, the Daly building, and other departments. There will be fewer telephones in use and the rates certainly will not decrease. The cost of electric light and gas has not come down; interest on mortgages has not come down; school fees have not come down; the rates of instalment payments have not come down; practically all contractual obligations have not come down. In this connection I shall quote from the Beatty report as follows: So rapid an increase in numbers, followed by so rapid a decrease, inevitably interferes with the smoothness of operation of the departments, and is a factor tending to reduce efficiency, at 
the same time that it causes innumerable problems of organization and classification, which cannot always be dealt with as rapidly as they arise.
And again:
The cost of living, which had already risen considerably from year to year since the beginning of the century, rose even more rapidly during the war years. In 1920, when the maximum was reached, foodstuffs were more than twice as expensive as they had been in 1913. The cost of living generally was 90 per cent higher than in 1913. Meantime, there had been no corresponding increase in civil service salaries. From 1913 to 1920, the average increase in civil service salaries was about 43 per cent, less than half as much as the rise in the cost of living. Since the salaries of the great majority of civil servants only sufficed, before the great rise in the cost of living, to keep them and their families in moderate comfort, it is easily seen that this failure of the average increase in salaries to keep pace with the rise in the cost of living involved a real hardship, during this period, for a considerable number of civil servants, for whom relief could only take the form either of resignation in order to accept better paid employment outside the service, or of a general revision of salaries which should have regard to the actual increase in the cost of living which had occurred.
These words should have been taken into account by those who have had to deal with matters of this kind. I continue:
Since the cost of living bonus had been calculated in relation to the needs of men with families, and had nothing to do with the merits of the services rendered by them, it of course acted as a levelling influence, reducing considerably the range between minimum and maximum salaries, and so narrowing the prospect of advancement in the service.
And in referring to the work performed at the present time by the service, the report
says:
It is safe to say that the tasks discharged by the civil service at the present time are very much greater and more-complex than they were in 1913; and these tasks have been undertaken by a service which is organized along the same lines as before the war, and with essentially the same structure. It is a tribute to the service as it now stands, that its structure has stood the strain so well.
The repeated blows it has received has sapped the foundation of this great institution. We hear a lot about the permanence and security of employment in the service, but in this regard I should like to quote from the Civil Service Review of December, 1931. The following is an article by a press correspondent:
Of course there is always the security argument. On more than one occasion, and under more than one administration when accompanying civil service delegations as representative of the press I have heard "high authorities" apply that blessed word "security" as a sort of salve or earwash against the sound claims of the service for long overdue salary revision.

The security of employment in the civil service cannot be valued or fixed by means of orders in council passed under peace, order and good government. The article continues:
But now even this security, like other well known securities, is not so secure as it used to be-witness what happened (and is still happening) in the Interior department.
And again:
Despite the facts of the case, however, the service has always been, and doubtless always will be, a favourite cockshy for such as are unable to find better sport or more useful employment; and of course, it is in the trough of periodic depression that the brickbats fly thickest and fastest. Just an old Spanish custom but frankly, as a newspaper man, I am at times unpleasantly surprised to find unwarranted and illogical attacks on the service in the columns of journals that might be expected to maintain a higher standard of editorial criticism.
I think these words could be applied to the words of hon. members on that side of the house, to which I hope to have an opportunity of referring on another occasion. The article continues:	.
With this in mind I would suggest that civil service organizations and well-wishers of the service generally should lose no opportunity to keep the press and the public better informed concerning the efficiency of the service and the value and importance of the work that is being done by civil servants in the interests of the people of Canada.
I come now to what I consider to be the gem in the speech of the Prime Minister. When the right hon. gentleman introduced the resolution upon which this bill is founded, he stated that he did so because the Minister of Finance was ill and regretted that he did not have an opportunity of preparing himself adequately for the occasion. I wonder what would have happened had the right hon. gentleman prepared himself a little more adequately? He is generally very .careful in the selection of his examples or citations, and I was surprised at his quoting the authority which he did. He quoted a letter which he had received from a lady, and I shall read it again. It is as follows:
It is now, and has long been, a cause of deep thankfulness that I have a salary to be cut, and that in these times of stress, when burdens are so great, not only in Canada but throughout the British Empire, whose honours and greatness we share and enjoy, that we can share and share gladly in the pinching. Ten per cent of my salary now seems but a small premium to pay for the security and comfort enjoyed by me in my years in the service. Since we have enjoyed the good years, shall we not also have the iean?
The right hon. gentleman read one letter. To even up I shall read a second one. Then
if he wants to even up by reading another, I shall read a third. Let me say that at this game I shall trump every ace he plays, and he may play with a deck of aces so far as that is concerned. The first letter I wish to read is as follows:
Is it possible that Mr. Bennett is going to cut the salaries of those who have hardly enough to live? I am a widow with three children, all of them going to school yet. I earn $900 a year. I pay $20 a month rent. I have managed to live with $55 a month but I have deprived myself of every pleasure; not even a picture show for years, but I was glad to do it. I managed to get an insurance policy to protect my dear little ones if anything happens to me. $7.50 less per month means years of sacrifices and privations for nothing, as I will be unable to continue to pay the premium. It would be different if I was alone, but there are the children. Can you do anything to stop this and see that justice is done?
You might as well stand on the beach and command the sea to stay where is it as try to stop this! This is somewhat different from the "pinched" lady who lived in security and comfort! But in order to have the Prime Minister even up with me, I shall read another letter:
As you are one of our representatives I suppose I have the right to write to you. I was interested to see the letter from the nice lady civil servant who was glad to be "pinched" to please the Prime Minister and save the country. I wonder if she gets the same kind of a pinch as I do? I am the wife of a letter carrier; my husband reached his maximum $1,500 per year this year past. He had to walk many thousands of miles through all kinds of weather in order to get to that high salary. Now they are going to take $150 off. We have four children all of school age; our present monthly salary cheque, after $6.25 for superannuation and $7.40 for insurance are deducted, is $111.35. Our rent is $25 and I do not think the Prime Minister will care to live in our house. Food for six of us costs $60. Heat and light comes to another $10; we can't afford a telephone. That leaves $16.25 for clothes, doctors' bills, recreation and all other expenses.
The Prime Minister and the Minister of Labour need not listen 'to this; their monthly expenses do not amount -to this:
Now, comes the cut of $12.50 per month. How can the Prime Minister expect my husband and me to enthuse! There are lots more in the same position as we are, thousands of us. Maybe I am not as patriotic as the nice lady, but my husband knows something about sacrifices for his country. He served for three years in the trenches in France. He risked his life then, like so many others and would do it again, but just the same the Prime Minister's horizontal idea of British fair play is not the kind that I was taught.
Would it not be more Christian and fair all around if some of the millionaires-like the

Prime Minister-and many other Canadian wealthy men would give up some of their many luxuries before making us give up our bare necessities?
The Prime Minister also said that he as well as all the other members of his cabinet had received similar letters from many civil servants, stating that they desired to make contributions in this time of stress. When this matter was under discussion before, the hon. member for South Perth (Mr. Sanderson) was speaking. At that time there were only a few ministers of the crown in their seats. The hon. member for South Perth asked the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. Ryckman) how many letters he had received, and he replied:	"None came to my department." The Minister of Railways (Mr. Manion) said the same thing. Those were the only two ministers who were present on that occasion. I wonder if the right hon. gentleman, after having put on the street hundreds of employees of the Interior department, a large number of temporary' employees, nearly 200 employees of the Department of National Defence and eighty-five employees of the Department of Public Works, after reducing the salaries of 12,000 civil servants in Ottawa; does not feel like opening the doors of his apartments and hearing what these workers of yesterday, the unemployed of to-day, have to say, rather than l'a:ll into rapturous ecstasy over the writings of a "pinched" lady. I wish just to paraphrase those famous words that have oft been quoted iu this house. "Let him open his door to the destitute widows, to the despairing fathers, to the imploring mothers, to the starving children. Let him for one day take contact with those who suffer. Let him take contact for one day with human misery! Then, were but one fibre of humanity left in the right hon. gentleman, he could not but put an end to this orgy of dismissals and of salary reductions." I think the words of the Latin poet are appropriate at this time:
Quos Jupiter vult perdere, dementat prius!
The Prime Minister came to Ottawa in July, 1930. He came to deliver what might be called the most important pronouncement of the Liberal-Conservative campaign in the political centre of Canada, the capital city. He came here for a distinct purpose: certainly it was not for the purpose of helping the Liberal cause throughout Canada: it was not for the purpose of helping the two Liberal candidates in this city. Throughout the campaign he had been most lavish in his promises, but when he came to Ottawa there

was no use in offering bridges, because we have all the bridges we need. There was no use offering free ports, because the Georgian Bay canal has not been built. He came to the city of Ottawa, the heart of the civil service of Canada, and so he talked of the civil service. This is what he is reported as having said, amongst others things:
Here dwell those who administer the departments of state. Here the major part of government is transacted. I have had a brief experience as a minister of the crown, but long as a member of parliament, and I would like to take the opportunity-
He never found the opportunity during the long time he was a member of parliament.
-of stating that the service rendered by the members of the government service in Ottawa has been and is invaluable.
That was no news to us in Ottawa, but it was a compliment well deserved and graciously expressed. He continued:
It has been said of the British civil service that it provides the stabilizing influence of government. That is true in Canada.
That was once true in Canada, but it is no longer true, not since the Prime Minister has started on his campaign of dismissal, salary reductions and general disruption of the service. He continued:
Good judgment and experience have always been placed at the service of the country. Canada must retain the services of its best brains.
Are we to infer from that that all those who have been retired, or will be retired, are the worst brains or have no brains at all? But that of course, was said on the eve of an election. He goes on:
We have them here-
Certainly, we know that.
-and we must see to it that those who forsake the greater remuneration of private business and turn a deaf ear to the' insistent calls and temptations of other countries, are not asked to pay too high a price for the loyalty and devotion which belongs to us.
But we must not forget this was said on the eve of an election. He talked then of loyalty and devotion! What does he say this year? At page 561 of Hansard of this year, introducing the bill providing for the salary cut, the Prime Minister said:
They could command a larger compensation in other walks of life, yet in these days it is apparent that the compensation given is not so much out of line as some people have thought. There is a measure of security of employment; there is a certainty of not too long hours.
In 1930 he talked of loyalty and devotion, and now he tailks of security of employment

and not too long hours. On the eve of the election he talked of "turning down higher salaries" in the outside world, and now he says that "the compensation is not so much out of line." 0 tempora, O mores! Loyalty and devotion on the twenty-sixth of July, 1930, and security of employment and not too long hours in 1932! Why, Mr. Speaker, speaking of security of employment, since the Prime Minister started his campaign of dismissals, you could not get Lloyd's or any other insurance agency for any premium to insure the security of a .position in the civil service.
The Prime Minister also said:
I make no distinction of class or race; it applies to all.
Why bring that up? He also said:
The civil service contains men and women equal to those in any part of the world.
Of course, that was said on the twenty-sixth of July, 1930, on the eve of an election. It looked then as though better remuneration for the civil service were in the offing. But to-day the Prime Minister says:
We must not ask them to sacrifice their future entirely.
No, Mr. Speaker, we do not ask them to risk their future, but we order them arbitrarily by means of this legislation to risk their future and everything that is sacred to them. But we are not to-day on the eve of an election. The Prime Minister continued:
That is equally true of those in the lower grades.
That was on the eve of an election, on the twenty-sixth of July. The Prime Minister knew that a large proportion of the civil servants belonged to the lower grades. He went on:
They are one in the great machinery that moves the government of Canada, everyone of them discharging as they do their duty and obligation to this country, and we render them homage for so doing.
We render homage-
-the gallant knight-
O see him stand His hat in hand,
His heart on his sleeve,
On this election eve.
Yes, that was on the twenty-sixth of July, on the eve of an election. But to-day the army of the dismissed and of those about to be dismissed now returns the gallant knight's homage, and in the words of the Roman gladiators about to enter the fatal arena they now cry, Ave Caesar! Morituri te salutant! Hail Caesar! Those about to die salute thee!
The lower grades! When the members on this side of the house said that the exemption of five per cent to those earning less than $1,200 and who paid into the superannuation fund was a sop, no truer word was spoken. When I asked the hon. Minister of Finance how many civil servants there were in receipt of $1,200 or less, he answered at page 901 of Hansard that there were 16,408. That seemed a formidable number. It seemed as though an army of civil servants would receive the benefit of the five per cent exemption. But I subsequently asked him how many of the 16,408 paid into the superannuation fund and . how many into the retirement fund, and he answered that 5,550 were paying into the superannuation fund and 550 into the retirement fund.
Subsection 2 of clause 5 of the bill makes it quite clear that the five per cent exemption will apply only to those who pay into the superannuation fund, and will not apply to those who pay into any other fund. So, after all, the benefit of the five per cent exemption will apply only to 5,550 civil servants earning $1,200 or less, and will not apply to 10,858 civil servants with a remuneration of $1,200 or less. It means that 10,858 civil servants with a remuneration of $1,200 or less will be called upon to pay the full ten per cent.
0	ye employees of the lower grades! On the eve of the election the Prime Minister rendered thee homage, but to-day, two years later, he cuts your salaries by ten per cent.
The Prime Minister also said on the twenty-sixth of July:
1	am not here to-night to make that kind of preelection promises.
Oh, no! On that sultry evening, butter would not melt in the mouth of the right hon. gentleman. He said:
All I. say is they are the same promises I have given to the people of Canada.
Don't the civil servants know it? Promises of what? Bridges, free ports, highways, and not least, the promise to end unemployment. The Prime Minister said:
I promise to deal fairly by them.
And the report in the Ottawa Journal shows that statement was greeted with cheers. Today that ought to be changed to tears. The Prime Minister went on to say:
To see that they have justice, and as a great chieftain of my party once said, a fair day's wage for a fair day's work.
That was true in those days, Mr. Speaker, but to-day there is not a fair day's work to

I have long since by personal investigation-
The right hon. gentleman has always been very strong on personal investigation:

satislied myself that all is not well to the extent that they would have it-
That is, that the civil servants had cause for complaint. He went on:
-and from my investigations and they are ConsiderableNothing small about the Prime Minister: -I have concluded-
What did he conclude? After these numerous personal investigations, and they were considerable, what did he find? Did he find that there was overlapping, overmanning, money being squandered? No, Mr. Speaker, he did not find that. All he found on the eve of the election was "All is not well to the extent that they, the civil servants, would have it." If there was overmanning at that time, surely his considerable and numerous personal investigations should have revealed it to the right hon. gentleman. If there was anything wrong at that time, why did he not find it out in his numerous personal investigations? If he did find out anything wrong, why did he not say so? Why did he wait until the introduction of this measure to say that there was overmanning and overlapping in the civil service? He did not then use these words which are to be found in Hansard of the twenty-sixth of February, 1932, at page 560:
That does not detract from the value of the service that is rendered by the painstaking and thoughtful men and women who serve the state with loyalty, and who do not look upon their positions merely as an opportunity to enable them to see what they can get from the treasury, but there are those who take that attitude, and ultimately that matter must be determined by suitable and proper investigation.
The right hon. gentleman did not find that out on the twenty-sixth of July, 1930, or if he did, he did not say so. Well, after his personal investigations, what did the Prime Minister conclude? He concluded (1) to add to the Civil Service Commission a member chosen from the ranks of the service itself; (2) to have the merit system rigidly adhered to; (3) to have a survey of all the civil service with a view to a proper reclassification, and the Prime Minister said " Such action will be taken at once, and not nine years hence." I will end unemployment, the Prime Minister said, and unemployment two years afterwards has not been ended. Nor 
has the Prime Minister made any attempt as yet to have the service reclassified. The Prime Minister also promised an amendment to the Superannuation Act to ensure equitable operation. But that was on the eve of the election, and no amendment of the sort has yet been brought down.
Just before I conclude I should like to put on Hansard a verse that I have just received: The Psalm of Bennett Bennett is my shepherd, I am in want,
He maketh me to lie down on park benches, He leadeth me beside still factories,
He restoreth my doubt in the Conservative party.
He leadeth me in the paths of destruction, For his party's sake.
Yea, though I walk in the valley of the shadow of debt
I will fear much evil, for thou art against me. The politicians and profiteers, they frighten me.
Thou preparest a reduction in my salary before me
In the presence of mine enemies.
Thou anointest my income with taxes;
My expenses runneth over my income.
Surely unemployment and poverty
Will follow me all the days of the
Conservative administration
And I shall live in a rented house forever.
For 'the reasons I have indicated I repeat that I am absolutely opposed to any cut in the salaries of the civil servants of Canada. I realize a considerable number of hon. members in this house feel that some reduction should be made; still I cannot agree with them.

subtopic: PROPOSED DEDUCTION OP TEN PEIS CENT IN INDEMNITIES AND SALARIES
speechtext:
We have heard of the
kindly old lady who wrote to the Prime Minister (Mr. Bennett) the letter which has since become so famous. The general public and the civil servants, however, are entitled to seek the cause of this legislation, and I have no doubt they will find that it is brought about through the failure of the high tariff policy of the Conservative party to cure the depression which is at the root of our trouble. To my way of thinking the so-called cut is simply a ten per cent extra income tax imposed upon public servants. Elementary economics teach us that taxation shall not be imposed on one particular class or community. Practical politics are found often to be diametrically opposed to that principle, and all through history isolated classes and communities have been specially picked out and made to suffer, as are the civil servants in Ottawa to-day. This is nothing new.
In August, 1930, the government changed its tune. Formerly it had said that the growing depression in Canada was due solely to alleged Liberal misrule, but in August it announced that the condition in Canada was only part of a growing world depression. I think the choice then presented itself of either advising private industry in Canada to maintain wages and salaries and thereby to maintain spending power, or to do the reverse.
The government chose to cut down salaries and dismiss employees. It must take the responsibility of giving a very definite lead to private industry throughout Canada. No government can escape that responsibility.
The example the government has set as to dismissals and salary cuts has been followed throughout Canada. This is a bankers' policy of deflation; it is being carried to an extreme, and the end is not in sight. If the government had called a conference of employers late in the year 1930 and had made an appeal to them, as did President Hoover of the United States, to maintain spending power by maintaining wages in my opinion Canada would be in a better position than it is today. Only private concerns already facing financial difficulties would have failed to follow that lead.
Very often hon. members in this house have quoted letters and books in support of their arguments. Instead of that I purpose to speak from my personal experience in some companies with which I am connected.
I happen to be a director of several Ottawa companies, and I am glad to say that more than two-thirds of those companies up to the present time have not reduced their pay-rolls or the number of their employees. Among these is the largest company with which I am connected. These companies decided that the maintenance of spending power in Ottawa would, in the net result, benefit them more than the discharge of employees, provided red figures could be kept at a reasonable distance from their ledgers. Another company of which I am a director, even before 1930, was worrying aibout the red figures in its ledgers, and the directors decided that the service -must be cut down by 30 per cent, or if the regular number of employees was to be maintained that the employees and management must take a ten per cent cut. There was an agreement that either one or the other course must be adopted. There was also unanimous agreement, however, that only one and not both of these courses would be followed. This company was operating in a position different from the others because it was working on a fixed tariff, extending over a period of years, its reserves were depleted and its borrowing powers were therefore much restricted. But it did not cut wages and dismiss employees as well; it did not, as an hon. member of this house characteristically stated, cut wages and also discharge forty per cent of its employees. A reference to the bureau of statistics will disclose the fact that the number of employees of this company has

Public Service-Salary Deduction
remained practically the same, except for the usual seasonal variation.
The government cannot, by any stretch of the imagination, be compared to a private company experiencing financial difficulties. No private concern has such enormous powers of borrowing or of taxation, yet the company of which I speak-and I know there are many others like it-chose to cut wages rather than discharge employees during the continued depression. The government of Canada is doing both, and I think that is the important point that should be remembered by this house. I do not think the actions of the big companies are absolutely typical of what is happening in Canadian industry; thousands of employers in Canada are maintaining employment and wages in spite of falling revenues, and those in charge of these concerns think they are doing a helpful and a patriotic work.
What will be the reaction to the lead of the government? What are employers in Canada going to think? Unless I am very much mistaken they will decide that the government would not adopt this course if it had any real hope that its policies would get this country back to normal within a reasonable time. How can this cold-hearted and panic-stricken move of discharging men and women and reducing wages be viewed except as a confession of failure? That is what the business men who have been maintaining wages and employment are saying to-day. They are also wondering,
I think, if they should delay very much longer in making cuts and dismissals, following the lead of the government, because naturally they feel that if the depression is going to last for several years they had 'better lay up reserves. I think the government is setting an example which will have its effect in every constituency in Canada. How many hon. members will be able -to return next session and say that men and women were not dismissed as a result of the example given by the government, and that as a result the purchasing power in their own constituencies has not been further contracted?
I suppose the action of the government will be popular with a certain type of individual, and it may be approved by a certain type of farmer. But it is a distinct threat to the farm hand, and no one who works for a wage or salary can fail to see the threat to that wage or salary in the wide-open invitation that the government is giving every employer in this country to-day.
For over two years the President of the United States has followed the policy of ask-
[Mr. Ahearo.J
ing private industry to maintain wages and salaries and thus help maintain purchasing power. The president has never deviated from this policy, and I believe that as a result hundreds of thousands of people in the United States are at work to-day instead of walking the streets. Only a few weeks ago President Hoover let it be known through the press of the country that he wished civil service salaries maintained, and he stated that he would veto any bills coming before him which had in view the reduction of salaries. I think no one in the United States is more anxious to bring into effect every reasonable measure of economy possible, but the president would not consent to the reduction of salaries. I am told the United States treasury faces a deficit of about two billion dollars, but in spite of that fact the president evidently realizes what an unwise lead to private industry would mean. I should like to quote from an article appearing in the Literary Digest of January 23, 1932, headed, "Swinging the Economy Axe." I think this illustrates my point;	[DOT]
Four representatives introduced bills to slash the pay of federal employees, who number more than 600.000. But President Hoover, strongly as he advocates economy, let it be known that he would veto any bill to reduce government workers' pay. He feels, the correspondent tells us, that such action would impair the efficiency of federal departments. . . .
This is the big point;
. . . . and set a bad example in private industry.
The Minister of Finance speaks of the 88,000,000 that will be saved by this special and extra income tax. What about the direct losses it is bound to cause? The government cannot make dismissals and wage cuts without this action being reflected in the national revenue. It will be almost impossible to compute, but I believe the loss to the treasury in the end will over-balance the gain, and the government will have a residue of unemployment, misery and discontent with which to deal.
I do not propose to enlarge upon the despair and the misery which will be caused to so many people in the city of Ottawa by the policy of the government as contained in this bill. I can only say that we feel it too deeply to say veiy much about it. Who can stand up and honestly say he believes this horizontal cut is equitable? Let us consider the case of a mail carrier receiving we will say 81,350 a year. First he gets a ten per cent cut, and then he loses his statutory increase, which makes a total loss of about 8255. In addition

Public Service-Salary Deduction
he must pay five per cent of his salary to the superannuation fund. Then let us consider the contribution of the cabinet ministers under this special income tax. On taking office their salary was S10.000 per year which, with their sessional indemnity of S4.000, gave them an income of 814,000. On that amount they will pay 81,400 by this special income tax. Since taking office in 1930 the ministers have had their government cars taken away from them by the edict of the Prime Minister and to make up for that the head of the state showed great compassion and allowed each minister S2.030 per year in lieu of a car. I understand that this amount is not taxed. Fifty dollars a month, or 8600 a year, will pay for a great many taxi rides, and we have some very luxurious taxis in Ottawa. Of course we are always delighted to see members of the cabinet on the Ottawa street cars, because it shows that they still have some spark of democracy left. Now consider the mail carrier and the twenty per cent contribution he is asked to make, and then consider hon. ministers. How can any man with any regard for equity and justice defend this bill? When you come to figure the financial sacrifice, it is the amount a man has left that counts.
When speaking on the resolution on which this bill is based, the Prime Minister referred to some remarks which I had addressed a few days previously to the Ottawa Liberal Twentieth Century Club. The right hon. gentleman chose to say that I was making political capital; I choose,to say that I stated facts. I suppose that what aroused the right hon. gentleman was the statement that the Liberals expect to win the traditional and almost sacred Tory county of Carleton, which has always selected a Conservative, no matter what his record in public life might be.
Ever since the ten per cent extra income tax was first announced by the Prime Minister, it has, I think, been quite apparent that every effort by the Liberal members to express disagreement with this bill has been met with the cry, "This is making political capital". The Ottawa newspaper supporting the government, or one that used to support it, set up that cry. When the hon. member for Shel-bume-Yarmouth (Mr. Ralston), who spoke from the heart, pleaded for those unfortunate men of the Royal Canadian Air Force who will soon be walking the streets, his successor in office replied to the effect that he was making politioal capital; and this was said in such unparliamentary language that I could not repeat his exact words without falling foul of you, Mr. Speaker.
If making political capital has suddenly become a major offence, does the right hon. gentleman think that his record in that respect entitles him to reprimand or rebuke anybody? Does he imagine that his remarks during the last general election campaign are gone and forgotten? Am I to take it that not one hon. member sitting on your right, Mr. Speaker, will attempt to make political capital out of this bill if it passes, nor that one Conservative newspaper will make any attempt in that direction? We on this side of the house, as a matter of fact, are not worried very much about making political capital, because hardly a week passes in these strenuous days when the right hon. gentleman himself does not supply us with all that we require.
To very many civil servants in the constituency which I represent, the passing of this bill will mean a double income tax. To the people of Ottaw-a it will mean the drying-up of purchasing power. To those unfortunate men and women whom the government is letting out, it will mean misery and privation. What a far cry from July, 1930: "We will end unemployment." Whoever thought that those who raised that cry would actually cause unemployment? The city of Ottawa, in a business sense, has been very adversely affected by the government's action in respect to the civil service. Perhaps nothing that has been done has so adversely affected the city as this government's statement that a survey will be made to ascertain whether further dismissals cannot 'be made. That statement hangs like the sword of Damocles over the head of every civil servant and, to a lesser degree, over the heads of all the citizens of the capital of Canada. What is to become of the men and women' who are being dismissed? If another $150,000,000 is to be spent by the dominion and provincial governments and by the municipalities under the same conditions that have obtained up to now, it means on the average less than a month's employment in the year, and at small wages.
This government came into power because it promised to end unemployment, and today, in spite of its election promise, the government of Canada is leading the way in cold-hearted dismissals of civil servants, and, in addition to that, it is bringing in this wage cut. In 1933 or 1934, when this parliament is dissolved and the Tory party composes its bedtime story for the campaign, does the right hon. gentleman imagine that the people of Ottawa will believe him again? If he does, he had better recall what President Lincoln*had to say with regard to the extent of the people's credulity.

Speaking to the resolution on March 3, I stated that the government, in introducing this legislation, was certainly setting a bad example to private industries, to contractors and to municipal and provincial governments.
1	did not think I was making any mistake in that regard, because I felt that private companies would certainly follow the example set by the government. I regret to say that my prediction has been justified. I have here an article that appeared in the Citizen of April
2	under the heading "Lower Wage Rates in effect by May is New Decision." I understand that contractors in the city of Ottawa decided at a meeting to follow the government's example. Let me quote exactly what was published in the Citizen:
"The contractors and other employers of labour in the building industries of this city have been considering for some time the relative value of the wages paid to employees in this industry, as compared with the existing cost of living, together with the cuts in salaries that have, and are, taking place in other occupations throughout the city. Finding the rate per hour is entirely too high in proportion, and also finding that under existing rates it is almost impossible for a prospective builder to receive any return whatsoever upon a commercial building, we feel that under the present conditions the public at large is paying too much for the necessary repairs and improvements that have to be done to keep their existing property from deterioration."
"We also consider that the existing rate, as paid to labour on civic work, is far too high, and take this opportunity of protesting against our civic authorities paying from five to fifteen cents per hour more than the rate paid by other industries. Having the interests of the public in view, the contractors have decided that the existing rates will be reduced from five to twenty-five cents per hour to take effect on May 2 next. It is our sincere hope that the residents of this city and district will appreciate the fact that it will give them the opportunity of having their work done at a greatly reduced cost, as already prices of materials have been materially reduced. The contractors feel, that, with these new rates, they will be greatly assisting the Mayor, J. J. Allen, in his commendable 'Work and Buy Campaign.' "
I certainly was not surprised at this move on the part of the contractors of Ottawa. I said on March 3 that I had been requested not only by the Liberal electors of my riding but also by the Conservative Association to protest against this legislation. One of the reasons given by these associations was the one I have given, namely, that if the federal authorities sought to save S8,000,000 by means of a horizontal cut of ten per cent, that example soon would be followed by private enterprises.
The employees of the E. B. Eddy Company in my own city suffered a cut last year, and although I cannot certify to my information,

I understand that this company intends to make a further cut this year. This is the largest concern in my constituency and ordinarily it gives employment to a considerable number of people. In addition to a cut in wages last year, these employees are to-day working only part time and are faced with a further cut.
The hardships borne by the civil servants in Ottawa and Hull do not seem to be known to the authorities. Over 12,000 civil servants in Ottawa and 500 in Hull will suffer this horizontal cut. Those receiving less than $1,200 per year will suffer the cut but have their superannuation paid. I believe the service will suffer because of this reduction. These men and women have been allowed to think that their salaries would be increased year by year, but this year they are not to receive the usual increase and are to suffer a reduction as well. As I said before, there are 4,000 employees in this city and vicinity who receive $100 or less per month, and these people will face a reduction of $60 in their annual salary. As stated by the hon. member for Ottawa (Mr. Chevrier) the prices of fuel, rent, mortgage interest and other contractual obligations have not decreased, but in fact have risen during the past year or so. Only three days ago the Department of Public W orks dismissed 102 of its temporary employees, and many of these employees who live in my city are to-day in the ranks of the unemployed. I have cited already the case of a father of eight children who after being appointed temporarily to this department decided to buy a home for his family. He invested all the cash he had saved at the time and assumed an obligation which to-day amounts to about $1,200. This man will not only suffer the loss of his position but must face the possibility of finding himself and his family out on the street. I have made representations to the department in this connection, but so far have obtained no results.
There is no use trying to find work in my city, as at present there are 3,000 unemployed. Some three or four hundred men receive one week's work per month, and the remaining 2,600 have no work and must live on charity. During last winter the city of Hull with the assistance of the provincial and federal authorities spent over $19,000 per month on direct relief. This will show to a certain extent what hardships this cut in the salaries will work on my constituents.
We in the province of Quebec are not used to these cuts in salary. The provincial government has taken drastic steps to balance its

Mr. Speaker, since this bill was presented I must confess that the more I think of it, the less I think of it. I wish the government would bring down something which I could support. For three or four weeks I have been opposing a most objectionable relief bill and now I am faced with another bill which is almost as odious. I have not been able to discover one redeeming feature in this legislation, unless it be the five per cent sop which is given to the lower grades. This is nothing less than an admission of the soundness of the graduated system; in fact, it condemns the bill itself.
I think there has been only one minister who has stood up to defend this bill, and no wonder. The Minister of Finance (Mr. Rhodes) undertook to defend it, and being the experienced and capable man he is in parliamentary practice and debate, it may seem like presumption for me to criticize his criticism. It was really a lamentable case he put up in support of the bill. I congratulate him for trying to father it, because before that it had been an orphan so far as the rear guard Tory forces of the house were concerned.
The minister said there was no difficulty in securing men and women for the lower classifications, while there is difficulty in securing and retaining those in the higher classifications. What does that mean? It means that it does not matter much about the lower grades because, according to the minister, or as the hon. member for Moose Jaw (Mr. Beynon) said the other day, " we can go out on the street and pick them up any old time." The higher classes are nurtured more carefully because they cannot be got every day and the government cannot be sure of keeping them. These reasons given by the Minister of Finance in support of this bill are not those which should be expected from a gentleman of his parts, and I do not think he. really holds that view. If I am putting a wrong interpretation upon his remarks I wish he would correct me right now.

I never did think
a maritime Tory was just quite as bad as an Ontario Tory, but what am I to think now?
The higher classes are being taken care of because there is difficulty in replacing them. That is given to us as a profound reason for supporting the bill. It was stated also that those in the higher grades donated to the income tax. Why should they not pay in both instances? To state that there should be a sort of saw-off because they are hit by the income tax is absolutely absurd. If lower classification escapes a cut, the minister said, a greater burden is thrown on the public. That was thought to be a cincher, but it is not. The same revenue can be secured out of the civil service on the principle of graduated cut, provided it is sharper at the higher salaries. So that is another piece of-what shall I call it?-nothing offensive, but a sort of highclass bit of piffle.
A graduated cut makes many inequalities, one at every grade, argues the minister. Of course it does. My hon. friend argues that it is better to have one great big differentiation between the lower and the higher paid ones than to have a number of small graduations. I never before heard that principle enunciated. If that were sound, how would you get along with your income tax graduation? How would you get along with all the grading in our wheat and cereals generally and other farm products? The closer the grades are together, the fairer the system, and the nearer you get to a sound and just graduated system. The same is true in this instance, but my good friend must have been in desperate straits when he pointed out that you would have a little inequality between each grade. If that is sound, how is it that every government that I know of except this one and one other, has had a graduated rather than a flat rate system of salary cut? Is his government right 'because it stands alone? Or is it wrong because this principle is unsound and has been proved to be so? I am very much disappointed with the Minister of Finance because I admire him greatly. What kind of defence would his colleagues and supporters have made if they had attempted to give one? They surely would have muffed it badly, because the bill is indefensible.
I am interested in this matter, not because I have in my constituency any more civil servants than any other member has in his I think I have one, but I take this ground, which I have always taken: I do not want to profess I have a tremendous amount of experience, but I cannot help having some. One who has been in parliament so long, whether he has made the best of his opportunities or not, cannot but have some knowledge of the civil service and the important part it plays in the

affairs of government. Since I have entered parliament I have heard the veriest nonsense talked in all parts of the house except perhaps from the corner to my left which is so eloquently silent now. We have heard about the civil service of Ottawa, the silk stockinged brigade on Wellington and Metcalfe streets and that sort of thing. Because the staff dressed respectably, it was apparently thought they were not doing anything. I am sorry to admit that long years ago-I shall not say how long-I used to hold such opinions myself ; but when we grow up we try to absorb some knowledge of affairs, although apparently some members opposite have not yet done so. I take the ground that it is more important to have a first class civil service staff and a second rate government, such as we have, than to have a second rate staff and a first class government, such as we have not. I do not. want to put the government in the second or third class; I shall just say an inexperienced government. We all have to be freshmen at some time or another and gain by experience, but there is not very much evidence of that experience developing yet in our hon. friends opposite. After long years on my farm in hiring men and women and my experience in the government of Saskatchewan as well as some here, I feel strongly about securing the very best staff that money will buy, using them well, paying them well and then expecting good service from them. That pays every time. At this time above all others it seems to me that principle should be carried out. But we are told the country's finances are bad; the budget must be balanced and therefore we have to go after the civil service staff and try to practise economy-that kind of so-called economy. I do not think that is economy at all. It is, as the old saying goes, saving at the spigot and wasting at the bung; penny wise and pound foolish.
Lest I be thought wrong, let me call to the support of my contention some of the findings and sayings of the Beatty commission. I do not think anybody has cast any reflection uipon the capacity of that commission to deal with the question of civil service salaries; my only regret is that these findings have not all been carried out. I am sorry to have to quote, but this is so good it is worth while, and lest my stand be challenged, I wish to support it with this testimony. I read this from page 9 of the report of the Beatty commission:
The formal distinction between the legislative and executive branches of government, between parliament on the one hand and the cabinet controlling administration on the other, obscures but it does not alter the fact that efficient

parliamentary government is only possible when the decisions embodied in statutory form are made effective throughout the Dominion by a body of trained administrators and experts. Until well within the nineteenth century, there was no country which possessed a trained civil service.
Therefore the importance and efficacy of our work in this legislative chamber depend upon a trained civil service staff to carry on the administrative services. Otherwise our legislation would be of no effect; we might as well have so much waste paper. Thus the administrative arm of government as represented by the civil service staff is a most important part of government. Because of that, this is not the time to weaken that arm; this is the wrong time to do so. Then, on page 10 of the Beatty commission report, I find this:
Throughout our inquiries, we have been impressed by the character of the work now done in the civil service of Canada. In accord with the highest traditions to be found elsewhere, its own tradition demands the faithful performance of his duties by the individual, though the results of the work done, however important they may be, do not accrue directly to him, either in the form of wealth, or, as a rule, in th" form of public recognition.
It is the service as a whole, whose prestige is increased, or whose influence for good is extended, when work of outstanding merit is performed; and it is within the service only that the individual worker obtains his reward. His reward is not in material advantage, but in the recognition and approbation of his fellow workers.
He gets merely a salary and the state gets the advantage and profit which is sometimes very great, of his work. On page 11 I find the following:
The importance of the responsibilities devolving upon the scientific workers in the Department of Agriculture, for example, it is almost impossible to exaggerate. In these days, when improvement of the quality of farm products is all important, their work is of lasting benefit to every farmer practising scientific agriculture, and to every organization marketing farm products. Much the same may be said, in a very different field, of the research work carried on in the Department of Mines by the staff of the Geological Survey and others. Many mining camps in Canada have presented new mining and metallurgical problems, upon the solution of which the development and economic use of their ores has depended.
That bears out my contention in full. Let me supplement it by another quotation from page 13 of the report:
In the course of discussions with deputy ministers and others who appeared to give evidence, we were impressed with the keenness and ability of many of the senior officers in the service. Their calibre is proof-if proof be needed-[DOT] that in the past the civil service has been successful in enlisting and retaining men of

Public Service-Salary Deduction
first-rate ability, despite the relatively moderate remuneration. We do not feel the same assurance, however, that it will continue successfully to recruit or hold such men in the future, unless conditions of employment and prospects of advancement in the service can be simplified and improved considerably.
That was said about two years ago, but the Beatty commission at that time took the ground, just as the Minister of Finance did, that it was difficult to hold good men, and they *were fearful then that they would not be able to hold them. Conditions have since changed rapidly, not due entirely to our friends opposite coming into power, of course, but reading this report I am bound to ask myself and the house this question : Are the conditions surrounding the civil service to-day conducive to holding men and getting good service, when the axe is now uplifted and threatening to strike at any time? The Prime Minister said that there were still too many in the civil service. Who knows who is going to be the next victim? Under such conditions how can you possibly get the maximum service from a staff, no matter how good it is?
I think I have quoted sufficiently from the Beatty report to show that the Beatty commission, a recognized authority, more than confirms what I said about the importance of the civil service. What did they say would be the cost of putting their recommendations into operation? They say:
We estimate that the net additional .cost in the first year will be approximately $360,000; and the total additional cost, when adjustment is completed, approximately $750,000 annually.
That would have secured the salary increases that were recommended for these 2,500 members of the scientific and technical service. A new classification was also made recommending increased salaries to various classes, but I shall not dwell on that except to say that the increases recommended run all the way from ten to forty .per cent of an increase for the 2,500 members of the technical staff. Then there was that vast body of civil servants comprising some fifty or sixty thousand whose salaries were also under consideration by the Beatty commission, with a view to having the salaries adjusted upwards or downwards as the case might be, although it was generally expected that the revision would be upwards.
There is another class of civil servants, the research workers on the staff of the bureau of research. These men are doing very, very important work. The then Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Malcolm) was organizing the bureau just about the time the Beatty commission started their investigation, and I observe that the Beatty commission in their interim report urged that the increases for the
staff of the research bureau be granted right away. That recommendation was carried out by the government, and it applied to about thirty or forty research men. They got their increase. Why? So that Doctor Tory and the Hon. Mr. Malcolm would be in a position to attract the very best men that good money could secure. By giving these men their raise right away, we got a good staff. Where is the fairness in applying a straight ten per cent salary cut to these men, who got their increase, and to the 2,500 technical men who were recommended for an increase by the Beatty commission, ranging all the way from ten to forty per cent, and who did not get it? And applying the cut also to that other great body of civil servants whose salaries were under consideration by the Beatty commission and who have received no increases, whose cases have not even been dealt with yet? I do not think, Mr. Speaker, that you could pick up sixteen men from the highways and by-ways who would make a worse muff of this job than has been made by this government. I cannot conceive that it would be possible.
How did the government go about it? I must largely absolve the Minister of Finance of blame, because at the time the decision was hastily made I do not think he was Minister of Finance. We know, of course, that estimates are dealt with a considerable time before the house meets, so the present Minister of Finance could not have had very much to do with it. There could be only one man responsible, and I do not think there is another man in Canada who would have thought of dealing with this matter in the way he has dealt with it. That one man, I am sorry to admit, is the Prime Minister. He made up his mind that the salaries of the civil servants were too high, and that ten per cent must come off, and without giving them a chance even to make a squawk the head comes right off by the shoulder. You must have noticed in your boyhood, Mr. Speaker, having been brought up on a farm- nearly everybody in politics claims to have been brought up on a farm-that when you go out and out the head off a cockerel-the axe is a very unscientific but a very sure way of doing the job-when the head is severed from the body the cockerel's mouth opens and gives a last gasp. That gasp is not very effectual. It is somewhat guttural, and accomplishes nothing. Now the civil service beads were cut off right by the shoulder before they were given an opportunity even to squawk. Of course the Prime Minister is a courteous gentleman, and when the civil servants asked for an interview it was granted, but on the very day that we were discussing
