the salary out in this house the civil servants' representatives trooped into a room in this building to present their views. Just imagine! Does any class of people in the world deserve that kind of treatment toy the Prime Minister of the country? I submit that they do not. Kicked around like old boots; that is what they were. The rest of the government must bear their share of the responsibility, however, whether they had anything to do with it or not, and they are bearing it and trying lamely to defend the government's course. The civil servants troop in and present their case to the Prime Minister, although it is already all over. Does the government think that the morale of these men will be improved by such treatment? Does the government think that the ship of state will be any safer in their hands, especially when the axe is still suspended over their heads? I lack words, Mr. Speaker, with which to express my utter disgust at such conduct towards such an important arm of government. I would not speak with such assurance, sir, if I did not know that that was the wrong way, from years of personal knowledge in dealing with government employees. Even if they were the most unworthy wretches under heaven, they did not deserve that kind of high handed, imperious treatment. Many of the staff are organized. Even the letter carriers and those workers who clean the rooms in this building are organized and the government could easily have consulted with them first and eased the blow. But there was another way to do it, and I am going to refer now to another Tory government to show apparently that good things can come out of Tory governments as well as bad things-I would be glad to say good things of this government and to throw a bouquet if I could only find an opportunity to do so. Up in Queen's Park, Toronto, they had the same sort of unpleasant duty to do. They desired to cut the salaries of the civil service, and how did they go about it? The premier of Ontario called in the heads of the civil service organizations. Every government should welcome every class of society that is organized, and should be ready to hear its representations on behalf of its many members. Well, in Ontario they called in the heads of the various civil service organizations and said in effect: We want you to sit down with us and assist us in doing an unpleasant duty which we think it is in the interests of the province to have done. And that was done. They did not adopt a flat rate, remember; no such nonsense as that, but a graduated system from top to bottom.

Have we heard any kick about it? Not one. What was that graduated system, Mr. Speaker? I must say I have been carrying the information around in my pocket ever since this bill came down. I find that to-night I am without it but I feel I know it well enough from memory to give some of the more important features. There was provision for a two per cent cut on the low salaries up to SI ,000, and there are about ten steps in the ladder. Of course from the standpoint of the Minister of Finance that will be an objection, if he is serious. The cuts run from two per cent on small salaries to twenty-five per cent, the latter on salaries from $10,000 upwards. If such a system were adopted here all the deputies with salaries of $10,000 would receive larger cuts, and if the same scale were used in this bill the ministers would be cut about 50 per cent instead of ten per cent as at present proposed. The rate in Ontario, however, stopped at $10,000, and all salaries over that figure were taxed 25 per cent. Had the same rate continued I repeat there would have been a out of 40 or 50 per cent on ministerial or other salaries of $20,000.
A survey of the salary cuts in Ontario raises the point that this question must have been viewed from a different angle by the provincial and federal governments. The government in Toronto viewed the matter from a fair, honest and just angle. Surely members of the federal government are not trying to save their own hides by taking the same cut as their most humble stenographer at $60 per month. If that is not the reason, what is it? What is more, Mr. Speaker, we learn from the schedules which have been worked out by the various organizations that not only are the lower paid servants to receive the same cut as the Prime Minister and his cabinet, but their cut is to be greater, even after allowing for the superannuation refund sop. In some cases the cut is greater by four per cent, depending upon the salary range. Those in the lower classifications in many cases are losing their statutory increases, plus the ten per cent. We can see the look of guilt on the faces of hon. members opposite, and especially on those of cabinet ministers, but they will commit this crime whether or not we object. We thus see that the humble charwomen and the post boys on the street are receiving greater percentage cuts than those of the cabinet ministers. This legislation is on all fours with the income tax outrage which was proposed last year by the government, but which fortunately for themselves was withdrawn. They would do well to-night if they were big enough to refrain from such a heinous crime against

Public Service-Salary Deduction
the lower grades of Canadian civil servants. No man living who has any heart in him at all can defend this measure; yet it will become law. Well, if there is a political gallows or a political purgatory there will certainly in due time be some contributions to it by hon. members opposite.
It is said, Mr. Speaker, that the world is in sad difficulties; no wonder, if there are many governments like this one. The ship of state is in danger. We remember a short time ago that one of our passenger ships ran on a reef at Bermuda, and on that ship were some of our Ottawa civil servants. I fancy if we had been on that ship in distress we would not have submitted to a lessening of the crew or have told them that they would be given hail Columbia later on regarding their salaries. That would be the time we should encourage them to do their duty. That is what we should do now: We should encourage the staff by simple justice and improve their morale instead of the opposite as the government are doing at present.
No wonder the countiy is wondering what will happen next. There is only one joy left to many in Canada, and that is that of guessing what hon. gentlemen opposite are going to do next-nobody knows. I do not wish to take too much time in a discussion of this matter, but hon. gentlemen opposite know they are deserving of my criticism and that is the reason they are saying so little- they have a guilty conscience. If I were doing them an injustice they would be howling like a lot of coyotes.
So it is that instead of having a staff at its top notch of efficiency, we have one suffering a deep sense of injustice. I do not have to go round looking for evidences of their views in the matter; I can hear them from all points -I do not need my audiphone to know that; I can hear it without any trouble. Some of the staff are wondering who is going to get the axe next. They are in a state of dread and anxiety; some of them are in almost despair.
As a rule the farmer, although he may be badly off, has enough to eat. True, some of them just now have hardly that much, but the great average class of farmers do not suffer from lack of food. The same does not apply to those civil servants receiving only about $80 per month. My hon. friends opposite know perfectly well there is a prejudice against civil servants because of misinformation on the subject on the part of so many people, and some of the general public also hold the mistaken idea that civil servants do not do very much work, when as a matter of fact
some of them are broken down with overwork. If we get more legislation like this, after the unemployment proposition, I do not know what may happen. Words fail to describe our indignation and disgust with this government, composed of men who are capable of better things and who know better. I have not one word to say against any member of the government as an individual, but some evil genius or evil spirit gets possession of them when they get together, and then there is the devil to pay.
Let us consider a certain family I know, consisting of two parents and four children. This man was on the canal first, until he reached his maximum of $100 a month. He was an ambitious young fellow, but he reached the limit of his salary range; children are a greater charge on the family budget as the years go by, so he decided to try to qualify for a higher classification. In order to do so. he had to go to school at night after working hard all day, but finally he started as a letter carrier at $85 a month, dropping $15 a month from his previous salary. He was given one increase, which brought his salary to about S90 a month, but while he was still getting $10 less than he had received previously, along came this legislation and he is now cut off from any further statutory increase, plus 10 per cent cut, or more than the Prime Minister is cut.	.

Before this amendment is put, Mr. Speaker, I feel that I should say just a word, even at this late hour. May I pay my respects to my hon. friend from Melville (Mr. Motherwell) who, perhaps unwittingly, paid me a veTy great compliment when he suggested that I might reply to his argument. Although my hon. friend treats the most serious subjects with levity, and sometimes in a most entertaining fashion, I know of no hon. gentleman who asserts bis views with greater vehemence. In fact, when the hon. member for Melville says a thing on his ipse dixit he rather leaves the impression with the house that t'he last word has been said. May I also say to my hon. friend-and I do so not unkindly-that he paid me a compliment when he said he was disappointed in the Minister of Finance. If my hon. friend had not been

1698	COMMONS
Public Service-Salary Deduction
disappointed in me I would have been disappointed in myself, because had it been otherwise I would have been afraid something was wrong with my course of action. You can always count on my hon. friend from Melville to be against the government.
But I notice, Mr. Speaker, that even my hon. friend is not infallible in his arguments. He proceeded to find fault with me because of an argument I used during an earlier stage of this discussion. In the first place let me say that he took from its context a sentence which I used on that occasion and put an interpretation upon it which it should not properly be given. I will let that pass for the moment, but I also brought forth the argument on that occasion with respect to the difficulty of securing permanency in the higher grades, and my hon. friend said that was mere piffle. Within two minutes the hon. gentleman proceeded to read from the report of the Beatty commission, after commending that commission as one with respect to which no criticism could be offered, and as a recognized authority. Then, if you please, one of the first things he read from that report was the very same argument I used on that previous occasion and which my hon. friend * called mere piffle.
There would be some merit in my hon. friend's argument if he were right in his assumption that this is a salary reduction. It is nothing of the sort, and I want to make that point very clear. The bill itself says in.terms that this is for one year, and the government has repeatedly asserted that the idea is to ask for a contribution from the civil servants for one year only. No one will be more delighted than the members of the government.-and I am sure I can speak for all hon. members of this house, on whatever side they sit-if a similar sacrifice is not called for in future years.
My hon. friend said that no government, admitting a cut or reduction to be necessary, would be so foolish as to follow the course taken by this government and make a level cut. Let me say .to my hon. friend that the very first act of the Liberal government when it came into power in 1897, when civil servants received salaries as low as $400 a year, was to deny to them their statutory increases for that year. That applied throughout the service, to the high man and the low man, and the government did it without statute or order in council; they just did it, in defiance of the statute which said that the civil servant "shall" receive an annual increase of so much.

speechtext: May I ask my hon. friend if that was not the war pension that was taken away?

subtopic: PROPOSED DEDUCTION OP TEN PEIS CENT IN INDEMNITIES AND SALARIES
speechtext: No, the statutory increases of all civil servants, as provided by statute in 1896; I have described the action taken by the Liberal government in 1897.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: PROPOSED DEDUCTION OP TEN PEIS CENT IN INDEMNITIES AND SALARIES
speechtext:
I am just using that as an illustration, to show that there was a level action taken with respect to every employee irrespective of salary; in other words, it was a straight reduction. I was merely dealing with the principle. As I said previously, if we are discussing this as a salary reduction which was to be permanent and which would have a bearing upon the salaries of civil servants I believe the matter would be entirely arguable, and for my part I would be prepared to discuss it upon its merits. But let me say again that we are asking for a contribution for this year only; this measure has no bearing upon the salary status of civil servants or upon their superannuation.
Hon, gentlemen opposite-and I do not find fault with them-have been rather at pains to take the attitude that this is rather a pleasant duty on the part of the government. I want to say that the government took this step with very great reluctance, but I also wish to point out to my hon. friend from Melville and to his associates that I have discussed the matter quite frankly with many civil servants, who realizing the gravity of the situation as it exists to-day, are prepared to make the sacrifice which the government, in the circumstances, has felt called upon to ask them to make. But I think, rather than be condemned, the government should receive some degree of commendation for taking their life in their hands and exhibiting enough courage to sponsor an unpleasant measure of this character. If we were after popularity, and wanted to help our peace of mind, we would ask for an increase in the salaries of the civil servants instead of asking that a reduction be made.
I do not propose to labour the argument at this hour of the night, especially as I discussed the question at considerable length during the better part of a day while the house was in committee on the resolution. With respect to the amendment, I have only this to say. No one knows better than my hon. friend who moved it, and who is a lawyer of parts, that irrespective of any merit

there may be in the principle of the amendment itself, it simply means that if his motion were passed it would have the effect not only of defeating the bill itself but would be a direct vote of want of confidence in the government. For that reason I must say to the hon. gentleman and to the house that we are unable to accept his amendment.

May I draw the attention of the house to the fact that whenever we have a vote and the pairs are declared, we take up a great deal of time, there is absolutely no order, and although pairs are supposed not to be recognized by the Speaker, at the same time they must be because the Speaker allows the members to declare themselves. Mr. BENNETT moved the adjournment of the house.
He said:	In order that business may be
expedited, we propose to-morrow, if we reach supply, to take up the remainder of the departments that have not yet been considered, and the convenience of the opposition will be studied as to which department it is desired to take as we proceed. There are, I understand, certain members of the opposition who wish to deal with different departments, and their convenience will be considered in that connection. So far as I am aware, the following departments have not yet been before the committee: Finance, Railways and Canals, Labour, Mines, Immigration and Colonization, National Defence, Interior, Pensions and National Health. There is the resolution on bankruptcy, and there are other government orders. If we reach supply we shall make the necessary arrangements to suit the convenience of the opposition as to which department they wish to consider.
Do I understand it is the intention of the government to take up any of the bills?
